newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Upside potential seen limited.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Upside potential seen limited.

text.p: The upside potential for the U.S. credit market is seen limited on Thursday as players stay tentative ahead of a meeting of the Federal Reserve's policy-setting body on March 25, analysts said.
"I think there's limited upside potential here in the market," said Dan Seto, senior economist at the Nikko Securities Co. International Inc.
The market has been rangebound for several sessions as players remain mostly divided on whether the Fed will tighten monetary policy at the March meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).
"The market is just sitting and waiting to see how the March 25 FOMC meeting comes out," said Paul Kasriel, chief U.S. economist at Northern Trust.

Players will have another chance to hear from the Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan on Thursday, when he testifies before the Congress' Joint Economic Committee on monetary policy. The event is expected to start at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.

Another top Fed official, governor Susan Phillips, will also testify on Thursday before the Senate Banking subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Regulatory Relief. The speech is also expected to start at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.

Traders will keep a close eye on those testimonies, but they said they have not gotten their hopes too high. "I don't think Greenspan will say anything new tomorrow. It's getting too close to the FOMC," one trader at a U.S. bank said.
Nikko's Seto said the market also has to take Greenspan's audience into account on Thursday.

"You've gotta keep in mind the people he's talking to. He's talking to a lot of politicians and a number of these politicians have already expressed displeasure about the possibility of higher interest rates," Seto said.
The Fed last changed monetary policy in January 1996, when it trimmed the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to the current 5.25 percent level.

The market will also take in some fresh data on Thursday, including the jobless claims report for the week ended March 15, the Philadelphia Fed business outlook survey for March and the January international trade data.
Analysts said the data are expected to confirm the current economic scenario, which involves moderate to firm growth, tight labor markets and low inflation.
"The data tomorrow will probably confirm what we already know. The focus now is on the FOMC meeting," said a trader at a foreign investment bank here.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond ended Wednesday's session down 10/32 at 95-15/32. Its yield closed at 6.99 percent, slightly below the 7.0 percent technical support barrier.

"It does appear that 7.0 percent is a tough level to go through on the bond. Maybe we're finding some support here," Northern Trust's Kasriel said. "But I just don't see this market rallying much from these levels."
On Wednesday, the Fed added temporary reserves to the banking system through overnight system repurchase agreements. The operation totaled $4.355 billion.
Federal funds are seen opening at 5.25 percent on Thursday.
